texts.gap.intro: Each arc is one breakthrough, coloured by where the research began: a university, a government lab or industry. It runs from the start of research to the first product, and a thinner arc continues to mainstream use where that followed.
texts.gap.example: For example: Penicillin. Research at a university began in 1928; the first product came in 1943, and mainstream use followed by 1946.
texts.gap.century: Here is a century of breakthroughs. Where mainstream use followed, the typical wait after the first product was 9 years.
texts.gap.trend: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has changed by no more than two years: 5 years for research begun before 1970, against 6 years for research begun since 2000.
texts.gap.heatchart: The heatmap shows how the typical gap from research to first product varies by field and by decade. Since 2010, Artificial intelligence has been quickest and Space slowest.
texts.gap.corrected: But much recent research has not yet reached a first product. Counting that unfinished work, the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about 7 years, which is not clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
texts.gap.gapchart: This chart tracks the typical gap decade by decade, then sketches possible scenarios beyond today, including ones shaped by AI and digital twins.
texts.gap.fields: Since 2000, AI itself has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product, at about 2 years. Select one field, as here with AI, and its sub-fields get their own tracks.
texts.gap.outlook: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically been quicker to reach a first product: 2 years, against 5 for the rest. Looking ahead, the estimates suggest AI-assisted work will be quicker: 8 years, against 10 for conventional work.
texts.gap.aichart: Each dot is one milestone, and the teal dots are AI-driven. For research since 2010, those typically took about 2 years to reach a first product, against 5 for the rest.
texts.gap.answer: So, is AI shrinking the gap? Two of the four measures here point to yes: exactly half. The answer updates as new evidence arrives.
texts.horizon.intro: The government's AI for clean energy vision is divided into several areas. Each diamond marks a story linked to one of those areas, and the stories play through in date order from 1980 onwards.
texts.horizon.radar: The AI Energy Vision Radar shows how close each area's technologies are to everyday use: 21 in research, 21 in pilots, 27 in early commercial use and 14 widely used. Already in use in Great Britain: 24.
texts.horizon.new: The automated search agents have recently found 18 new items, including SPP tariff for economic topology optimisation. Mark them as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.
texts.horizon.next: Over the next five years, 34 products are expected. The soonest is AI in grid control rooms, around 2027, and Security, assurance and governance has the most on the way.
texts.horizon.pipechart: The pipeline chart follows each technology from its area, through its readiness, to whether Great Britain has deployed it. So far, 24 of 83 have been deployed there.
texts.horizon.changes: The Forecast drift chart, for clean energy only, tracks when each technology is expected to arrive. Each time the agents revise an estimate, the change appears here, so you can see which forecasts are holding steady and which have moved.
texts.horizon.slide: For a briefing, the PowerPoint report window creates a single-slide summary, ready to drop into a deck.
texts.horizon.answer: So, what is on the horizon? A busy pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are closest to everyday use.
texts.secure.intro: New technology can give attackers fresh ways in; together these form the attack surface. This filter keeps only technologies that widen it, 61 per cent of everything tracked, from smart grid-edge devices to AI agents.
texts.secure.lens: The Cyber lens estimates how long security took to catch up with new technology. Only 19 cases are researched with a source; the rest are rough guides from related milestones. Typical wait: 2 years.
texts.secure.secchart: This chart shows how many years technologies waited for a security response. Apart from 19 researched cases, bars are rough guides drawn from related milestones, not researched facts. The longest wait shown is 78 years, for Westinghouse Televox: telephone-commanded robot.
texts.secure.gaps: Gaps are hard to judge yet: most technologies here have not had their own security response researched, so the chart shows the nearest related security milestone as a rough guide. The agents are researching them, most recent first.
texts.secure.example: This card names a risk and ways to reduce it, linked to recognised guidance: the National Cyber Security Centre's Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), Ofgem's CAF Overlay, plus NIST guidance from the US, North America's NERC CIP and international IEC 62443.
texts.secure.guidance: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications. The latest: Cyber Assessment Framework: Core Profile (v4.0).
texts.secure.caution: This tour draws on AI-assisted research meant to prompt discussion; it is not security advice. Always involve qualified experts, and your regulator where relevant.
texts.secure.answer: So, is security keeping pace? Security is catching up faster than it used to.
texts.fortune.intro: Research does not just change products; it can also make fortunes. This chart, Time to a fortune, follows founders from starting a company to the stock market listing, sale or valuation that made them rich.
texts.fortune.research: Of 86 fortunes here, 38 began with work in a university or research lab. For those founders, research brought not only new products but also their wealth.
texts.fortune.speed: The journey from founding to fortune looks shorter: about 12 years for companies founded before 1970, against about 3 years for those founded since 2015. But recent companies still on their way are not counted, which may flatter them.
texts.fortune.fortchart: Watch the race unfold through time. Each bubble is a fortune, sized by net worth. Gold rings mark founders whose companies grew out of research: 38 of 86.
texts.fortune.fastest: Sorted by speed, the quickest journey so far comes first: Thinking Machines Lab, which took under a year to go from founding to fortune.
texts.fortune.uk: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK took 8 years to reach a product, slower than the 6 years in the rest of the world.
texts.fortune.uni: Now the filter shows university projects. Those yet to reach a product number 7; any still on their way could become breakthroughs, and perhaps fortunes, in future.
texts.fortune.table: The Table lists every milestone. Sort by any column, such as the gap between milestones, and select a row to read its story.
texts.fortune.answer: From lab to fortune: the journey from founding a company to a fortune looks to be getting shorter, though many recent companies are still on their way.
texts.how.intro: This model is kept up to date by AI agents, automated programs that run every week. So far it holds 691 milestones.
texts.how.research: A research agent searches for new breakthroughs and products across every field of AI, including each area of AI for clean energy. Everything it adds appears in the 'Data changes' view.
texts.how.qa: A second agent checks each new entry independently. It requires more than one source, and the quoted evidence must really appear on the cited page. Nothing is ever deleted.
texts.how.more: Further agents track new security guidance, shown here in the Cyber lens, and keep these walk-throughs up to date. Every change must pass automatic checks before it is published.
texts.how.quality: The 'Data quality' view shows that 69 percent of records now cite a checked source. Each forecast is recorded now and will be scored against what really happens once the outcome is known.
texts.how.labels: Each record carries a label showing how it was produced and checked: source-cited, AI-compiled or AI estimate. Use the Filters panel to show only the records with the labels you want.
texts.how.arrange: Pick a ready-made view to arrange the panels for exploring, presenting, analysing or an AI for clean energy briefing. Save your own under My views, which are kept in your file. Any view can be shared as a link.
texts.how.whatifchart: The What if? chart gives rough estimates, not firm predictions. It shows how much sooner technologies not yet available might arrive if AI speeds up steps such as discovery, simulation and approvals. An agent updates the underlying research weekly.
texts.how.answer: Use Help on the toolbar, or any 'i' button, to find out what each feature does. Because AI maintains this model, it may contain errors, so check anything important against the original sources.
texts.week.intro: This week's analysis, updated 3 Nov 2026, 08:44. The agents added 204 milestones this week, including Zuse Z1: First programmable binary mechanical computer and goddard's first instrument-carrying rocket.
texts.week.w1: Google Project Suncatcher TPU satellite in orbit began as a Google design study of solar-powered AI chips in space. This month a prototype reached orbit, and Google says it booted, ran a prompt and returned a haiku. An early proof, not a fleet.
texts.week.w2: Bepirovirsen: first antisense drug for hepatitis B began as an Ionis drug designed to block the virus's genetic messages, later licensed to GSK. US regulators approved it this month. In final trials, a minority of patients were functionally cured, against none on placebo.
texts.week.w3: Is AI speeding things up? Since 2010, 46 AI-driven milestones typically took 2 years from research to first use, compared with 5 for everything else. Treat this as a hint, not proof: AI milestones are fewer and more recent.
texts.week.w4: Security often trails the technology it protects. This week brought new guidance on moving to post-quantum encryption. Across 279 milestones, the typical lag is 2 years, and 14 gaps remain open. The longest wait was Westinghouse Televox: telephone-commanded robot, at 78 years.
texts.week.w5: In AI for clean energy, corrections now record silicon solar cells, utility-scale wind and grid-scale batteries as deployed in Britain. A milestone on dynamic rating of Britain's power lines was also added. Of 83 items, 14 have reached scale and 21 remain in research.
texts.week.w6: Size-adjustable pediatric heart valve (Autus) grew from Boston Children's lab work on a valve that expands as a child grows. After a first implant in a young patient and a larger trial, US regulators approved it this month, and Edwards bought the company.
texts.cleanweek.intro: AI for clean energy: this week's analysis, updated 3 Nov 2026, 08:45. The agents added 18 clean energy technologies this week, including SPP tariff for economic topology optimisation and fully autonomous wind-blade inspection and repair robots.
texts.cleanweek.c1: Start with speed. Since 2010, the 46 AI-driven milestones took a median of 2 years to go from research to real use, against 5 for the rest. The AI group is small and the evidence is mixed, so treat this as a hint, not proof.
texts.cleanweek.c2: The pipeline holds 83 clean energy technologies: 21 in research, 21 in pilot, 27 in first commercial use and 14 at scale. 24 are used in Great Britain. Checks also scaled back a claim: liquid air storage moved from commercial to pilot.
texts.cleanweek.c3: Some ideas did move forward. AI assurance for energy, which is about checking that AI systems used in energy can be trusted, moved from research to pilot this week. Its status in Great Britain also changed from planned to trial.
texts.cleanweek.c4: In the what-if scenario, practical AI levers would bring 33 clean energy technologies into real use by 2030, against 32 expected now. planning, connection and operations is the strongest lever. This is a modelled scenario, not a forecast.
texts.cleanweek.c5: Finally, trust. 5 clean energy technologies still have no researched security response, and these open gaps are listed first. A second AI model also disputed a good share of this week's new entries, so those stay flagged until they are checked.
texts.charthow.open: This is the Gap explorer. Use the tabs at the top to switch charts; your filters apply to all of them. Select a milestone to open its story, and What if? will jump to that same milestone.
texts.charthow.gapsort: Here the Gap explorer is sorted and zoomed in. You can sort and colour the bars in different ways. Drag across the chart to zoom into a span of years, and double-click to reset the view.
texts.charthow.filter: The filter bar narrows any chart by search, field or origin; here it shows energy only. With fewer items on screen, each row gets taller and the timeline zooms in to fit.
texts.charthow.heat: In the heatmap, each cell holds a group of milestones. Select a cell to list them in the side panel, which stays open while you read a story.
texts.charthow.ai: In AI vs the rest, drag across the chart to draw a box and zoom in. Milestone labels appear once there is room. To list a group of milestones instead, switch to select mode.
texts.charthow.pipe: The pipeline follows technologies through their stages of development. Select any bar or flow to list the technologies behind it.
texts.charthow.drift: In Forecast drift, each bar counts the milestones expected to arrive in a given year. Select a bar to list them. Trails show how a milestone's expected date has moved each time its forecast was revised.
texts.charthow.sec: Security lag shows the wait between a technology and a security response. Open gaps come first; you can also sort by arrival or longest wait. Only 19 responses are researched with a source; the rest are rough guides from related later milestones.
texts.charthow.fort: Press play to watch the race to a fortune unfold over time, or select a bubble to read that company's story.
texts.charthow.whatif: What if? shows how arrival dates could shift when practical AI levers are applied. The ambitious scenario is on screen. Switch scenario or adjust the levers, then select a row to see the reasoning and any research behind it.
texts.charthow.insight: Finally, back on the heatmap, the Insight callout summarises what the chart shows, and can be read aloud with subtitles. Select any number in it to see where it comes from. You can also save any chart as an image or a CSV file.
texts.kiosk.wait: Welcome to The Shrinking Gap from Research to Change. A century of research breakthroughs is playing now, from first research to real-world use. Touch the screen to explore it yourself.
texts.kiosk.desnz: This view follows AI for clean energy. The AI Energy Vision Radar shows how ready each area’s technologies are, and what is arriving next. So, what is on the horizon? A busy pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are closest to everyday use.
texts.kiosk.analysis: The findings dashboard brings the headline results together. So, is AI shrinking the gap? Two of the four measures here point to yes: exactly half. The answer updates as new evidence arrives.
texts.questions.clean-ai: We track 47 AI-driven clean energy technologies, listed here. Of these, 8 are already used in Great Britain and 15 are still in research. Of the AI for clean energy areas on the radar, Asset planning, operation and maintenance has the most.
texts.questions.clean-next: 34 clean energy technologies are expected by 2031. 7 of them are already in use or on trial in Great Britain; the rest would be new here.
texts.questions.ai-faster: Since 2010, AI-driven research has taken about 2 years to reach a first product, against 5 for everything else. That is quicker, but it rests on only 46 milestones so far.
texts.questions.fields: Since 2010, Artificial intelligence has been quickest, at about 2 years from research to first product, and Space slowest, at about 15. Communications has sped up most since the 1990s.
texts.questions.security: As a rough guide, security protections have arrived about 2 years after the technology they protect; some figures are proxies, not researched dates. Only 19 have a researched security response so far, so treat any gaps as provisional.
texts.questions.whatif: If AI were used to speed up development, technologies still to arrive could come about 0.5 years sooner on average. By 2030, 112 could have arrived, against 111 on current trends. The biggest lever is simulation and digital twins. This is an illustration, not a forecast.
texts.questions.slips: 142 forecasts are being tracked. None has been revised yet. The agents re-estimate each week, so any delays will show up here.
texts.questions.fortune: Of 86 fortunes tracked here, 38 started in a university or research lab. The quickest was Thinking Machines Lab, made in under a year. Recent fortunes are being made more quickly than earlier ones.
texts.questions.changed: The agents added 204 milestones this week, including Zuse Z1: First programmable binary mechanical computer and goddard's first instrument-carrying rocket. 535 records were corrected or updated.
